messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Rajesh Patel

Rajesh Patel was thirty-eight when the traffic stop changed everything. He had been driving home from a late project deadline at the design firm in downtown Portland, the city lights blurring past his windshield as he thought about the presentation he'd nailed that afternoon. A police car pulled behind him on the Morrison Bridge—he wasn't speeding, he was certain of that—but his stomach tightened anyway. The officer approached the driver's window with a flashlight, and Rajesh's hands went cold on the steering wheel. What started as a routine license check escalated when the officer claimed to smell marijuana. Rajesh, who had never used drugs in his life, tried to explain, his voice climbing higher as he protested. The officer's hand moved to his belt. Another car arrived. For forty-five minutes, Rajesh was removed from his vehicle, patted down, questioned about gang affiliations he had no connection to, and treated with a contempt that seemed to have nothing to do with anything he had actually done. Eventually, they let him go—no charges, no apology—but not before one of the officers made a comment about "people like you" that Rajesh couldn't quite parse, though he understood the intent perfectly.

Three years later, Rajesh carries that night like a stone in his chest. The specific smell of burnt rubber from the officer's patrol car—a sharp, acrid odor that lingers in his memory—now appears everywhere. He catches it on the street and his body floods with adrenaline. The smell of burnt plastic in his own kitchen when he's cooking triggers an immediate, visceral panic. His wife, Meera, has learned not to ask him why he flinches. What terrifies Rajesh most is what that night proved to him: the world is fundamentally dangerous, and the people meant to protect it cannot be trusted. He was betrayed not by a criminal but by authority itself, by someone whose job was to serve him. This certainty—that the system is rigged, that people in uniform are threats regardless of his own innocence—now colors everything. When he sees a police car, even parked on a side street, his mind floods with danger signals. Any person in uniform, a security guard at the grocery store, a parking enforcement officer, triggers the same cascade of fear and rage.

Over the past three years, Rajesh has developed intricate ways of managing this world he now understands to be hostile. Before any interaction—a phone call to his insurance company, a meeting with a client, even casual conversation with a neighbor—he rehearses what he will say. He scripts it out in his head, sometimes aloud in the shower, playing both sides of the dialogue. He is hypervigilant in public spaces, tracking the location of anyone in uniform, noting exits, assessing threats. He avoids driving on certain routes because they pass police stations. He has stopped planning for the future. When Meera suggests a vacation next summer or asks about renovating the kitchen, Rajesh feels a creeping dread. To make plans is to assume safety, and he cannot afford that assumption. The uncertainty feels safer than hope.

The weight of rehearsal and avoidance has warped his memory of the event itself. When he tries to tell someone—his therapist, his wife, a friend—what happened, the words scatter. He knows the sequence, the timeline, the officer's face, but when he opens his mouth to explain, something fractures. He loses the thread midway through, his voice becoming mechanical, and he cannot finish. The harder he tries to articulate it, the more the memory fragments into disconnected images: the flashlight, the hand on the belt, the phrase "people like you." When he remembers the event in quiet moments, an overwhelming guilt settles over him—a guilt that makes no rational sense, since he did nothing wrong, yet it persists. This guilt, paradoxically, drives him to rehearse more, to plan less, to scan more carefully for danger. Each avoidance, each rehearsal, each moment of hypervigilance reinforces his conviction that the world is unsafe and that he cannot trust anyone with authority—which then makes him more attuned to uniforms, more reactive to burnt smells, more convinced that another encounter is inevitable.

Rajesh came to his first therapy appointment last month because Meera issued an ultimatum. His avoidance has begun to cost him work; clients sense his anxiety, his need to control every interaction. He has turned down two promotions because they would require him to attend industry conferences and networking events—spaces he cannot monitor, cannot predict. He is forty-one now, and he is afraid that if he does not find a way to reclaim his life, he will spend the rest of it small and trapped, rehearsing conversations that never quite happen, avoiding a future that might have been safe all along.
